title: The point gains power: thirty upgrades for Vectors & Forces
status: Design proposal only; current thirteen-hall order retained. No runtime, tutorial.md or final.md changes. Source inspection is not a runtime test.
premise: You bring the familiar point into a wing where you first describe a movement, then influence a body, and finally work with the consequences left in the room. Each apparatus makes a promise you can test. The same point can arrive precisely, miss, or leave a situation worth using next.
compression: SAME POINT + SAME CUBE. 13 core lessons + 12 practice + 5 optional extensions. PROMISE → PREDICT → RELEASE → REVEAL → RESIDUE. Describe → influence → work with what happened. Keep quantity/frame/receiver exact. Retain aftermath with explicit recovery. Invite observation; preserve agency. Verify rules, not a required catastrophe.

acts.title: I. Describe the journey
acts.story: The point is familiar. What changes is how you describe its relation to another place. You learn to preserve a direction, combine a route and decide which part of a gap matters.

acts.title: II. Give the point motion
acts.story: A predicted arc reaches across the room. Then the point keeps a velocity after your command ends. The same object becomes a thruster; now you must learn how to arrive.

acts.title: III. Meet the room
acts.story: The room has its own conditions. Identical arrows produce different receiver responses. Surfaces resist, channels guide and a released point continues beyond the apparatus.

acts.title: IV. Let one event reach another
acts.story: A spring returns the point. Another body receives its movement. Cycles can align or drift, and the conveyor makes delay accumulate into an altered room.

acts.title: V. Other bodies answer
acts.story: Attraction affects more than a nominated target. A source may also move; a support may cease to support. The student encounters bodies with their own conditions of stability.

acts.title: VI. Make another way through
acts.story: A deflection opens a passage and leaves the obstacle somewhere else. The final task asks the student to use learned operations and the actual remaining arrangement. Work with what happened becomes an independent capacity, with several valid solutions.

halls.title: A relation I can carry
halls.tutorial_summary: Revisit the point and line. Move both endpoints together, then change their separation. The learner distinguishes a position, a displacement and its displayed arrow; a unit direction becomes available for later aiming.
halls.reflection_question: What survives when a relation moves?

halls.title: One destination, more than one journey
halls.tutorial_summary: Join two displacements using the familiar point. Compare the resultant with the travelled route, then make another route to the same place. This prepares addition of compatible velocity or force contributions without treating them as the same quantity.

halls.title: What part of the relation matters?
halls.tutorial_summary: Use a moving target to construct a gap, compare directions, and resolve the gap along a rail plus a remainder. Keep projection as the main code lesson. Dot-product aiming is a return; the lever is a preview whose physical dynamics arrive later.

halls.title: A prediction crosses the room
halls.tutorial_summary: Give the point an initial velocity and compare the predicted path with a chosen receiver. Use the already supplied trajectory runner; name gravity and starting conditions without teaching an entire solver. A launch-pad crossing lets the player experience the same trajectory idea.
halls.reflection_question: What did the prediction assume about arrival?

halls.title: The point keeps moving
halls.tutorial_summary: Continue with an actual dynamic point. Apply a finite force, release it, brake it, and compare masses. The new lesson is retained velocity under force. Two held points then reuse normalization and addition to provide the agreed thrust ability.
halls.reflection_question: What continues after the command ends?

halls.title: The room answers
halls.tutorial_summary: Give two receivers the same spatial vector: one takes it as velocity, the other as acceleration. Reuse the point's state instead of replacing it with a fresh particle system. The vortex combines radial and tangential contributions as practice.
halls.reflection_question: Does an arrow command a speed or change it?

halls.title: Contact changes the journey
halls.tutorial_summary: Carry the moving point into contact and resistance. Keep velocity-dependent drag as the new code lesson; use friction, an incline and a transparent curved channel as controlled comparisons. Make each model's constraints visible before adding spectacle.
halls.reflection_question: Which histories does a model keep or erase?

halls.title: A relation pulls back
halls.tutorial_summary: Attach the point to a visible anchor. Extend it and release; compare return and damping while retaining velocity. Colliding spring balls and a hinged bridge are applications or optional joint studies, not prerequisites for understanding the spring.
halls.reflection_question: What happens when the place of return can move?

halls.title: One cycle changes the next
halls.tutorial_summary: Reuse a known movement to make two cycles meet. Separate phase from rate in the small lesson, then use the conveyor's input and receiver rates to make accumulation visible. A robot-arm duet is an optional interpretation with supplied controllers.
halls.reflection_question: Can two successful tasks prevent a shared result?

halls.title: The source is also a body
halls.tutorial_summary: Upgrade the familiar point into a bounded attractor. Begin with one target, then compare a held source with a released source receiving the opposite interaction force. A three-body comparison is an optional later experiment.
halls.reflection_question: What was being supported while the source looked fixed?

halls.title: A body needs support
halls.tutorial_summary: Place the known cube on finite supports; shift its mass distribution and release it. Make the static balance prediction and its limits explicit. The four-legged character is a supplied extension, whose commanded gait must not be mistaken for physical balance.
halls.reflection_question: Which capacities does a body need to remain here?

halls.title: Other bodies have conditions
halls.tutorial_summary: Use the point's projectile to redirect a dynamic target, with selection and occlusion shown separately from collision response. Reuse known impulse and momentum; the new lesson is the receiver's eligibility and state. A bowling layout offers a quiet practice version.
halls.reflection_question: Must making a passage mean destroying a body?

halls.title: The experiment becomes a place
halls.tutorial_summary: Deliver the point through a local acceleration field using the available tools. First compare the same field's cube and visitor adapters; then compose launch, brake, guide and support. The student chooses a route and explains its consequences.
halls.reflection_question: What can we do with the room we have changed?

ideas.title: The arrow you can carry
ideas.question: Does the relation change when both points move?
ideas.upgrade: Use the familiar black point as the movable endpoint. A paired handle shifts both ends; the arrow and two wall projections follow. Recall the unit-direction operation; idea 2 isolates it as practice.
ideas.carried_forward: Point, coordinates and line.
ideas.precision: Both endpoints translate together while their difference remains unchanged.
ideas.possible_consequence: A wall projection can shrink although the three-dimensional gap stays the same.
ideas.source_status: The hall already has the room-reading vector and projection study.
ideas.implementation_work: Add recognizable point handles and one shared displacement readout; preserve the existing geometry model.
ideas.acceptance_check: Translate both ends by the same offset and assert equal displacement; verify a changed gap and declared display scale.

dramaturgy.promise: Carry this relation elsewhere.
dramaturgy.prediction: Will its length survive moving both ends?
dramaturgy.release: Finish a paired translation; leave both points at their new positions.
dramaturgy.reveal: The same difference appears at another location.
dramaturgy.residue: Keep a ghost of the original pair and the relocated pair for comparison.

ideas.future_dramaturgy_check: Check that the intended goal and decisive event are visible, compare at least one baseline success and one lawful alternative, retain the declared evidence, and verify the specified recovery. Do not require a particular failure or disable general player control.

ideas.title: Aim without changing strength
ideas.question: Can a longer pointing gesture keep the same direction?
ideas.upgrade: Pair the long displacement arrow with a unit arrow carried by the same point. Change length, then direction; at coincident endpoints show no available direction.
ideas.carried_forward: A direction reused by aiming and thrust.
ideas.precision: Long and short nonzero gaps produce the same unit direction.
ideas.possible_consequence: Coincident points cannot supply a direction; a visible threshold prevents an invented aim.
ideas.source_status: The normalization study already uses a 0.001 magnitude threshold and reference sphere/rings.
ideas.implementation_work: Connect the familiar point input; retain and disclose that threshold rather than silently changing it.
ideas.acceptance_check: Above threshold, unit length and collinearity; at/below threshold, documented zero result.

dramaturgy.promise: Keep the aim while changing the gesture.
dramaturgy.prediction: Will doubling the gap double the unit arrow?
dramaturgy.release: Set a length, then stop adjusting.
dramaturgy.reveal: The direction agrees while the unit magnitude stays fixed; coincident points expose the threshold.
dramaturgy.residue: Retain one long and one short input beside their unit directions.

ideas.future_dramaturgy_check: Check that the intended goal and decisive event are visible, compare at least one baseline success and one lawful alternative, retain the declared evidence, and verify the specified recovery. Do not require a particular failure or disable general player control.

ideas.title: Two moves deliver one point
ideas.question: Where do these two movements take it?
ideas.upgrade: Extend vector_addition_walk into a delivery diagram: two placed displacement arrows carry the point to a marked plinth. Reveal the single resultant.
ideas.carried_forward: The same endpoint and displacement values.
ideas.precision: Two legs end at origin plus a plus b.
ideas.possible_consequence: A reversed contribution changes the destination; the cancelled route may still have travelled a distance.
ideas.source_status: Walked and console addition studies exist.
ideas.implementation_work: Add destination/route comparison around their arithmetic; this remains prescribed displacement, not force simulation.
ideas.acceptance_check: Assert endpoint equals origin+a+b, including opposing inputs; label units as metres.

dramaturgy.promise: Deliver the point with two instructions.
dramaturgy.prediction: Mark where two arrows together will end.
dramaturgy.release: Commit the two prescribed displacements.
dramaturgy.reveal: The point reaches the sum, including a return to its start when contributions cancel.
dramaturgy.residue: Keep both route legs and their resultant; label this prescribed movement.

ideas.future_dramaturgy_check: Check that the intended goal and decisive event are visible, compare at least one baseline success and one lawful alternative, retain the declared evidence, and verify the specified recovery. Do not require a particular failure or disable general player control.

ideas.title: Same arrival, different journey
ideas.question: Can two routes finish together and still differ?
ideas.upgrade: Save two short routes for the point, both ending on the same plinth. Keep their traces, lengths and encountered obstacles beside the shared resultant.
ideas.carried_forward: Trace records and the sum from the previous encounter.
ideas.precision: Two different routes agree on final displacement.
ideas.possible_consequence: One passes behind a screen or crosses an occupied space; a shared result does not promise the same experience.
ideas.source_status: The installed addition route already distinguishes travelled distance from the result.
ideas.implementation_work: Reuse the Trace sample contract for a second bounded route; no automatic cross-hall persistence is assumed.
ideas.acceptance_check: Compare equal endpoints, distinct recorded paths and summed segment lengths.

dramaturgy.promise: Find another way to the same place.
dramaturgy.prediction: Will equal destinations mean equal journeys?
dramaturgy.release: Commit the second recorded route.
dramaturgy.reveal: The endpoints coincide while route lengths and intermediate positions differ.
dramaturgy.residue: Preserve both bounded traces.

ideas.future_dramaturgy_check: Check that the intended goal and decisive event are visible, compare at least one baseline success and one lawful alternative, retain the declared evidence, and verify the specified recovery. Do not require a particular failure or disable general player control.

ideas.title: The target moved
ideas.question: What remains between the point and its destination?
ideas.upgrade: Continue the shared gap room with the familiar point and a movable target cup. Moving either updates target minus source; swap them to reverse the gap.
ideas.carried_forward: The same two positions, later used by attraction.
ideas.precision: The arrow reaches the target from the source.
ideas.possible_consequence: Moving the destination changes the instruction even though the point has not moved.
ideas.source_status: A bounded room_gap station and shared gap/projection data already exist.
ideas.implementation_work: Restyle endpoints as the carried point and receiver; keep the existing bounds visible.
ideas.acceptance_check: Subtract, swap, coincide and shift both ends; assert sign and translation invariance.

dramaturgy.promise: Reach the cup that has moved.
dramaturgy.prediction: Predict the new gap before revealing its arrow.
dramaturgy.release: Place the cup and stop editing.
dramaturgy.reveal: The gap changes; moving both endpoints together leaves it unchanged.
dramaturgy.residue: Keep the earlier gap as a labelled comparison, not a second active command.

ideas.title: The rail keeps only part
ideas.question: How much of this gap lies along the rail?
ideas.upgrade: Make the projection station a small delivery rail. Show the point's along-rail destination and leave the perpendicular remainder visible as a second line.
ideas.carried_forward: The gap from the previous encounter.
ideas.precision: Along component plus remainder recovers the original gap.
ideas.possible_consequence: A point on the rail can be as close as this rule permits and still miss the target.
ideas.source_status: The installed room_projection already exposes a unit rail, retained component and remainder.
ideas.implementation_work: Add a clear receiver at the projected position; treat the rail as a geometric constraint here.
ideas.acceptance_check: Assert recombination and perpendicular remainder, including reversed rail and zero gap.

dramaturgy.promise: Bring the point as close as this rail permits.
dramaturgy.prediction: Choose the place on the rail you think will be nearest.
dramaturgy.release: Commit a rail direction and reveal the projection.
dramaturgy.reveal: An along-rail result leaves a visible perpendicular remainder.
dramaturgy.residue: Retain the gap, its component and its remainder together.

ideas.title: The receiver is looking elsewhere
ideas.question: Is the point inside the receiver's cone of attention?
ideas.upgrade: Replace the dot_aligner's implied combat with an aimable receiver and a visible acceptance cone. Put the point ahead, sideways and behind before trying a threshold.
ideas.carried_forward: Unit directions and signed dot.
ideas.precision: A clearly aligned point is accepted.
ideas.possible_consequence: The nearest point can remain outside the receiver's chosen direction.
ideas.source_status: DotAligner renders angular cases and a slider-driven classification; it is not a verified moving sensor.
ideas.implementation_work: Add actual point/controller directions and a declared threshold; keep distance and occlusion separate.
ideas.acceptance_check: Check dot values for parallel, perpendicular and opposing directions, plus threshold boundaries.

dramaturgy.promise: Let the receiver recognise your point.
dramaturgy.prediction: Predict acceptance at the edge of its cone.
dramaturgy.release: Hold one aim and commit a sensor sample.
dramaturgy.reveal: Acceptance follows the declared angle threshold; near does not necessarily mean eligible.
dramaturgy.residue: Keep the sampled directions and decision until the next trial.

ideas.title: Where you push will matter
ideas.question: Which applied direction can turn this lever?
ideas.upgrade: Keep torque_crank as a geometric preview. Move the indicated application point and direction; compare parallel and perpendicular cases, then mark its later hinge return.
ideas.carried_forward: The relation r cross F, reused with real dynamics later.
ideas.precision: The preview identifies the same moment from a long weak and short strong push.
ideas.possible_consequence: Pushing along the lever can show zero moment despite a large force magnitude.
ideas.source_status: Current crank is a static angular-factor diagram with generated readouts, not measured rotational dynamics.
ideas.implementation_work: Improve the preview labels now; physical hinge response belongs to idea 22 after Motion.
ideas.acceptance_check: Verify vector cross-product direction and zero parallel moment; do not test a rendered angle as an angular acceleration.

dramaturgy.promise: Choose a push that could turn the lever.
dramaturgy.prediction: Compare along-arm and across-arm directions.
dramaturgy.release: Commit one geometric comparison; no dynamic release is claimed.
dramaturgy.reveal: The displayed cross product distinguishes moments, not measured angular acceleration.
dramaturgy.residue: Keep the two force/arm diagrams for their later physical return.

ideas.title: The cup across the room
ideas.question: Will this initial velocity reach the receiver?
ideas.upgrade: Keep the launch chamber's analytic predictor and place a cup at its proposed landing. Reuse the point appearance; compare high and low paths before enabling a physical trial variant.
ideas.carried_forward: The direction, magnitude and saved trace.
ideas.precision: A trial with matching declared assumptions reaches the predicted neighbourhood.
ideas.possible_consequence: An intervening ring contact changes the physical flight beyond the collision-free prediction.
ideas.source_status: An analytic launch chamber and separate catapult artifacts exist; their matching is not yet verified.
ideas.implementation_work: Build a controlled comparison with matched initial state and gravity. Full force accumulation is explained in Motion.
ideas.acceptance_check: Check sampled trajectory and landing height; compare a no-contact dynamic trial within a declared integration tolerance.

dramaturgy.promise: Land the point in the cup.
dramaturgy.prediction: Mark the expected landing before launch.
dramaturgy.release: Launch from the declared initial velocity; the collision-free predictor stays visible.
dramaturgy.reveal: A clean arrival agrees with the model; a ring collision introduces a condition absent from it.
dramaturgy.residue: Keep the actual resting point and a bounded predicted/observed trace comparison.

ideas.title: Your body follows the arc
ideas.question: Can you land where you sent the point?
ideas.upgrade: Put a short launch-pad course beside the sphere trial: generous platforms first, poles over the existing void only as an optional challenge.
ideas.carried_forward: The known launch setting applied through the player adapter.
ideas.precision: A clear launch and landing complete the crossing.
ideas.possible_consequence: The correct destination with excessive arrival speed carries the body onward.
ideas.source_status: Player launch artifacts exist; receiver behavior differs from the analytic point.
ideas.implementation_work: Declare whether each pad sets launch velocity or adds impulse; one activation per entry; desktop/VR adapter and landing checks.
ideas.acceptance_check: Assert the chosen launch policy and re-entry behavior; test collisions and a recoverable landing before the void.

dramaturgy.promise: Land where the point landed.
dramaturgy.prediction: Judge arrival velocity as well as the destination.
dramaturgy.release: Enter the pad; keep ordinary player controls and the declared launch behavior.
dramaturgy.reveal: A measured arrival stays; an overshoot may continue beyond the correct landing position.
dramaturgy.residue: Keep the landing/flight trace when feasible; recover the player explicitly after a fall.

ideas.title: Let go of the command
ideas.question: Does the point stop when the push stops?
ideas.upgrade: Upgrade motion_chamber with the familiar point beside its cube. PUSH, COAST and BRAKE retain their distinct meanings; a visible trail records the result.
ideas.carried_forward: One dynamic point, later used for thrust and targets.
ideas.precision: A timed push followed by braking stops near the chosen mark.
ideas.possible_consequence: COAST leaves velocity; the point can pass its intended destination.
ideas.source_status: A real RigidBody3D pulse/coast/brake chamber exists with private collision layers and a bounded trail.
ideas.implementation_work: Add a same-contract sphere receiver; preserve the isolated baseline before opening it to room props.
ideas.acceptance_check: Off contact and without damping, compare delta-v to F*t/m; COAST retains velocity; BRAKE opposes it without an authored overshoot.

dramaturgy.promise: Bring the point to the mark.
dramaturgy.prediction: Predict what will continue after the force pulse ends.
dramaturgy.release: Let the timed push expire, or choose COAST.
dramaturgy.reveal: Velocity remains; braking is a further intervention.
dramaturgy.residue: Keep the point's state and bounded trail until a deliberate reset.

ideas.title: Same push, different body
ideas.question: Which body changes its velocity most?
ideas.upgrade: Give equal-sized point receivers different explicitly labelled masses. Apply the same timed force and compare velocities before comparing collisions.
ideas.carried_forward: The force scheduler and receiver from Motion.
ideas.precision: The measured velocity change follows the selected mass.
ideas.possible_consequence: A visually identical point is harder to accelerate because an invisible parameter differs.
ideas.source_status: Motion already cycles 1/2/4 kg; an additional mass study exists.
ideas.implementation_work: Use Motion's actual receiver for side-by-side comparison; keep damping and contacts controlled.
ideas.acceptance_check: Hold force/duration constant; test inverse mass response. Do not suggest heavier objects fall faster under common gravitational acceleration.

dramaturgy.promise: Give both points the same opportunity.
dramaturgy.prediction: Predict which equal-looking mass changes velocity more.
dramaturgy.release: Apply equal timed forces under matched conditions.
dramaturgy.reveal: Different masses acquire different velocity changes.
dramaturgy.residue: Keep the two trials and their declared mass/force values.

ideas.title: Two points can carry you
ideas.question: Can two hands give you one controlled flight?
ideas.upgrade: Continue the point as a thruster in each hand. Aim down/back and press triggers to rise/advance; change one hand, release both, then counter-thrust to land.
ideas.carried_forward: The familiar point becomes a reusable player ability.
ideas.precision: Balanced contributions produce an intended approach and landing.
ideas.possible_consequence: Releasing one hand changes the sum; releasing both leaves motion and gravity.
ideas.source_status: Catalyst and XR receiver adapter exist; dual-point flight is still proposed.
ideas.implementation_work: One movement owner sums both inputs. Define mass/gravity/strength and a separate firing mode; resolve catalyst auto-return explicitly.
ideas.acceptance_check: Each release removes only that input; no duplicate integration or velocity reset; compare desktop and synthetic XR before headset validation.

dramaturgy.prediction: Predict the sum of the two thrust directions.
dramaturgy.release: Release one or both triggers; steering and counter-thrust remain available.
dramaturgy.reveal: The contribution ends while motion and gravity continue.
dramaturgy.residue: Retain the approach trace and settings; player recovery never depends on watching a cinematic.

ideas.question: Will gathering the point bring it to the centre?
ideas.upgrade: Begin with one sphere and a radial attraction; add a tangential contribution. Then release a few loose cubes and let entry speed change the result.

ideas.upgrade: Build a shallow incline comparison from the wedge/ramp family. First release the same body with rotation locked and free; only then compare the sphere and cube.

ground_rules: Preserve the identity/look of PointBody and the inherited cube. Extend behavior where compatible; do not claim that current independent artifacts already share one runtime instance.

Declare the state handed between halls: body configuration, learned tool modes and selected trace/experiment records. Implement the transport explicitly; do not assume live nodes survive a map unload.
Every visible arrow names its quantity and frame: displacement in m, velocity in m/s, acceleration in m/s², force in N. Compatible quantities may be added; their types are not interchangeable.
Opening mathematical models can be prescribed geometry. Label them; compare with physical receivers only after defining the different contracts.
One owner integrates each body. Never add a custom velocity/position integration on top of a Godot rigid-body solver that already advances the same state.
Keep player camera orientation level and separate tracked motion from software propulsion. Physical headset comfort remains a later test, not guaranteed by desktop assertions.
Give each core tutorial one rebuildable focus and print its complete changed code plus an exact reference to inherited code. Core success includes an independent changed example.
Reflection asks what a rule retains, excludes or makes possible. It need not explain every museum artifact; optional apparatus can remain outside both written tracks.
Do not stage numerical failure as evidence of a force. Tunnelling, unstable joints and fake deformation are not substitutes for a tested mechanical relation.
Leave aftermath inspectable, with an explicit reset. Bound active bodies and reveal that capacity; a test must not demand a specific collapse.
Noise, flocking, fluid pressure, cloth, robot inverse kinematics and physical quadruped locomotion remain later topics or supplied systems.

The thirteen core lessons depend on earlier core knowledge. Practice provides additional attempts; extension concepts are never prerequisites for the core route. Listed idea dependencies are knowledge/behavior dependencies, not a promise of shared runtime code today.
Use the dramaturgy rules for release, observation and residue. They are proposed interaction contracts; historical traces and live bodies are not silently assumed to survive a hall unload.

delivery.phase: 1. Confirm the spine of the lesson
delivery.detail: One agreed paragraph and reconstructable lesson per existing hall. Review the abstract/analytic/physical distinction before expanding full code.
Establish the dynamic point and selected persistence contract, verify launch versus force, then implement the approved two-hand thrust in the existing museum.
Upgrade one field, one channel, one spring pair, the conveyor and one target; each has a baseline success and a retained aftermath.
Choose extension specimens after the core route works. They must not become prerequisites for finishing the basic force tutorial.

verification: Future mechanism and dramaturgy checks are specified per idea but not run. Proposal checks cover completeness, the unchanged role/hall/dependency structure, five beats per idea, source existence, protected-file hashes and report links. No claim of human comprehension, runtime physics or headset testing.

dramaturgy_rules: Promise → prediction → release → reveal → residue. These are design beats, not compulsory screens, dialogue or timed steps.
Keep the goal and decisive contact within a readable view; subtle cases may need optional arrows, a trace or a replay. Do not assume an uncaptioned viewer can understand every force.
For a small physical trial, aim for a readable 5–20 second reveal where appropriate. Setup, reflection, continuous flight and orbit studies have no universal time limit.
Release means an action has consequences that continue. It does not mean disabling locomotion, grabbing, counter-thrust or emergency recovery. Let natural travel time create the pause.
In the opening geometry halls, release is committing a comparison or prescribed route. Do not manufacture a physics event to satisfy the five-beat template.

Preserve aftermath by default when a trial ends in a miss or jam. Separate deliberate artifact reset from player respawn, lost-object recovery and finite simulation capacity; disclose recovery and retain evidence where feasible.

Residue is first an actual arrangement, remaining motion, configuration or bounded recorded trace. Dents, abrasion, torn material, fused bodies and tangled rope require separately implemented receiver models.
Mathematical predictions remain conditional. A collision outside a collision-free launch model changes the conditions; it does not refute the model.
Spatial spectacle and tutorial role are separate. The optional hinged bridge can be a major encounter without becoming a prerequisite for the core course.
Promise and precision stay credible: show a baseline success, not a machine rigged to collapse. Test mechanisms, records and recovery; do not assert an exact gag as the learning outcome.

feedback_decisions.reason: Added concrete promise, prediction, release, reveal and residue to all thirty cards; geometry remains geometric.

feedback_decisions.topic: An explicit change in the student's attitude
feedback_decisions.reason: Added three attitudes across the existing thirteen halls, with spatial consequences. Kept the six-part teaching route and all role/dependency decisions.
Marked ten scene groups using eleven existing idea IDs. Visual prominence does not promote the optional bridge into a core lesson.
Preserve inspectable aftermath by default, with declared exceptions for player recovery, lost objects and capacity. Do not promise infinite state or prevent an exit.
Invite a pause through flight time, distance and clear view. Keep movement and available corrective actions; interruption becomes another recorded cause.

feedback_decisions.topic: Every event manufactures a damaged artifact
feedback_decisions.reason: Begin with actual arrangements, motion and recorded paths. A friction trail is not abrasion, two oscillators are not automatically a knot, and a cluster is not a fused mesh.

feedback_decisions.topic: Every scene reads silently in 5–20 seconds
feedback_decisions.reason: Use it as a target for simple physical reveals, not a hard timing, accessibility or comprehension claim for every lesson.
Precision and lawful alternative outcomes both count. Separate model limits, selected conditions and numerical errors. Tutorial code reconstructs one focus; reflection can follow the aftermath.
